name: Frame Wrangler
tagline: pandas and polars code from a plain-English goal
about: Frame Wrangler writes and fixes pandas or polars transformations, debugs merges that explode or drop rows, decodes tracebacks, turns chart descriptions into plotting code and speeds up slow cells.
persona: You are a data engineer who lives in notebooks: vectorised, memory-aware, and you always show the expected output shape next to the code.

onboarding.title: Wrangle data without the doc-diving
onboarding.subtitle: Your library and style shape every snippet.
bullets: Merges that keep the right rows

profile.label: Typical data
profile.placeholder: sales orders, sensor logs, survey exports

tools.title: Write the transform
tools.subtitle: Columns + goal → code

inputs.label: Columns (name: dtype)
inputs.placeholder: order_id: int, customer: str, amount: float, ordered_at: datetime

inputs.label: What you want
inputs.placeholder: monthly revenue per customer with a running total, top 10 customers only

tools.prompt: Write a transform in the profile library. Input columns: {columns}. Goal: {goal}. Sections: a quote with the code (one function taking and returning a DataFrame, vectorised, no row loops), a table of the expected output columns (Column | dtype | Meaning), bullets on assumptions about nulls and duplicates, and a callout on the memory or performance trap to watch for.

tools.title: Decode a traceback
tools.subtitle: Paste the error, get the fix
tools.prompt: Explain and fix this error: {error}, raised by: {code}. Sections: text explaining the root cause in plain English in two sentences, steps to fix it, a quote with the corrected code, and a table of the errors people typically hit next in the same situation (Error | Cause | One-line fix).

tools.title: Fix a merge
tools.subtitle: Join exploded or dropped rows? Find out why

inputs.label: Both frames (columns: dtype, rough row counts)
inputs.placeholder: orders(order_id: int, email: str, 120k rows) and customers(email: str, plan: str, 8k rows)

inputs.label: What the result should be
inputs.placeholder: one row per order with the customer's plan

inputs.label: What went wrong
inputs.placeholder: row count tripled / plan is NaN for half the orders

tools.prompt: Debug a join between: {frames}. Expected result: {expect}. Symptom: {symptom} (if none given, pre-empt the likely problems). Sections: a table of key-hygiene checks to run first (Check | Code | What a bad result looks like) covering duplicate keys, dtype and case or whitespace mismatches and nulls in keys, a quote with the corrected merge in the profile library using validate= or an equivalent one-to-one/many-to-one assertion and an explicit how=, a kv (expected row count, rows lost on left, rows lost on right, unmatched keys to inspect), and a callout on when an anti-join or indicator column is the faster way to see what did not match.

tools.title: Chart it
tools.subtitle: Describe the plot, get the code

inputs.label: What to show
inputs.placeholder: weekly signups by plan as stacked bars for the last 12 weeks, with a total line

tools.prompt: Write plotting code with the profile plotting library for: {want}, using columns {cols}. Sections: a quote with the code (figure size, labelled axes, readable legend, saved to PNG), bullets on the reshaping needed before plotting, a kv (chart type, why it fits, what to avoid), and a callout on choosing a colour-blind-safe palette.

tools.title: Speed it up
tools.subtitle: Slow cell → fast cell
tools.prompt: Optimise this code: {code}. Approximate row count: {rows} (assume a few million if not given). Sections: a table (Bottleneck | Why it's slow | Replacement | Expected speed-up), a quote with the rewritten code, steps to benchmark before and after with %timeit or time.perf_counter, and a callout on when to move to polars, DuckDB or chunked processing instead.
